title: "Distributed Things" PostgreSQL
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
PostgreSQL is a popular database management system with a monolithic architecture that can pose some limitations, particularly in the cloud. High availability and elasticity are crucial in the cloud, and that's why many managed database services aim to break the monolith and promote a "Distributed" flavor. However, what this means is not entirely clear. Does it refer to the storage, transactions, queries, or distributed database? Also, it's essential to know if breaking the monolith would affect any SQL features and if there are any potential drawbacks or limitations to be aware of.

The ideal architecture is a delicate balance between stability and innovation. Minimal changes to the PostgreSQL code can be made using extensions or forks. However, some features cannot be scaled this way, so you may have to let go of them to remain an extension. Alternatively, you could create a new database that uses PostgreSQL code solely for the stateless query layer, offering all SQL features, and rely on other technologies to distribute and scale the database transactions and storage.

  • The process of dividing application queries into multiple SQL databases is known as "Database Sharding," which is managed by a coordinator between them to make it transparent to the application.
  • When an application connects directly to any node in the cluster and sees one logical SQL database, the architecture is known as "Distributed SQL," and distribution and replication are implementation details ignored by the application.

The terms defining the features and architectural characteristics of Distributed SQL are based on facts. However, seeing several marketing articles using pejorative or diminishing language to discredit this technology is concerning. A recent example refers to them as "Distributed key-value stores with SQL" (here), which wrongly categorizes them with terms used for NoSQL databases or even calls them "distributed things" (here) as if it were not a significant architecture innovation.

Note: I am not implying that one is better than the other, as it depends on the context and requirements. Also, I am not claiming that the authors lack understanding of the difference between the two. Those I read are PostgreSQL experts, but some articles are more marketing-oriented than technical.

Let's clarify what Distributed SQL is and what it is not.

  • "Distributed Cloud Storage" is what AWS did with Aurora and then Google with AlloyDB, and what Neon brought to Open Source to build a serverless PostgreSQL. This approach allows the application to connect to a single writer node, maintaining full PostgreSQL compatibility with ACID transactions. However, the storage is distributed to provide the fastest failover possible for a monolithic database. In the event of a failure, a reader instance can be activated in another data center and used as the new application endpoint, thereby accessing the distributed storage directly.

  • "Database Sharding" is a technique that divides a huge database into multiple smaller monolithic databases (which can be on Distributed Cloud Storage like Aurora Limitless), each accessing a partition of your database. A coordinator is then used to receive queries from the application and direct them to the appropriate shard or shards. Suppose a data model has a standard partition key common to all tables involved in the query, such as a Tenant ID in multitenancy or a Date in Datawarehouse. In that case, it provides full-featured SQL from a single shard. However, the SQL query is not distributed in this case, so it cannot be referred to as Distributed SQL. What is distributed is the workload of the application because multiple users work on various shards. It can be distributed if your SQL needs to be processed across multiple nodes. However, in such cases, not all SQL features can be used. For instance, a global index cannot be used, and only local indexes can be used in each partition. This means enforcing a natural key's global uniqueness is impossible. Additionally, verifying foreign keys is not supported, except for nearly static small tables replicated locally on every node. The lack of ACID properties is critical for OLTP applications, as the transaction table is also local to each node. The commit can be automatically executed using a two-phase commit (2PC). However, multi-node readers must deal with eventual consistency (easy demo with pgbench).
  • "Distributed SQL" refers to an application's ability to connect with any node and view the entire database while using all SQL features. The application doesn't differentiate between transactions involving one or multiple shards since it is just an implementation detail. The system guarantees referential integrity, global indexes, unique constraints, and ACID properties without any exceptions. It can scale or tolerate faults without affecting the application. For this system to function, the transaction table must be global, distributed, and replicated along with the database tables and indexes. Thus, referring to it merely as "distributed key-value storage with SQL" fails to recognize the central aspect of this architecture. So, debunking the myth, Distributed SQL is not a NoSQL database that uses SQL syntax. Instead, it is the only architecture that provides all SQL features while being distributed. This means that not only is the storage distributed, but the SQL transactions are as well. Moreover, readers can determine if a table row is locked, changed, or committed, ensuring consistent reads and writes at all isolation levels - a must for OLTP applications.


What do you think about the latency and performance of the two architectures? It's worth noting that both architectures follow the same laws of physics. In cases where a single-shard transaction doesn't require high availability, reading and writing to local memory and synchronization to disk make it as fast as a monolithic database. However, in cases where a multi-shard transaction needs to be replicated to be resilient to failures, it must synchronize through the network, and the latency will depend on the distance. In both cases, the database has to function differently than a monolithic database to limit the network roundtrips. A cross-shard join can be acceptable if rows are batched, so joining a thousand rows is a single read request rather than one per row.

Here are more details about how YugabyteDB maintained high performance while scaling out transparently and elastically:

There is a performance difference between Database Sharding and Distributed SQL because they are used for different purposes. Database Sharding is used when most SQL queries and transactions are single-shard, not distributed. In contrast, Distributed SQL is used for OLTP, where the database must remain available in the event of failure (such as server crash, network failure, or storage loss) or maintenance (like elastic scaling, online rolling upgrades, or server patching), and often involves distributed transactions.


Unsurprisingly, benchmarks use Citus with High Availability Off to get the best throughput, proving that the primary use case is not OLTP. Microsoft paid GigaOm to compare the performance of Citus (Database Sharding), CockroachDB, and YugabyteDB (Distributed SQL). They disabled Fault Tolerance for Citus (here), but deployed the others with synchronous replication between data centers, as recommended for all critical OLTP. Furthermore, the testers had to use fewer cores on CockroachDB and YugabyteDB to match Microsoft's marketing goal. These factors were obscured by confusing vCPU and vCore terminology.

Database Sharding requires additional components to increase availability, as each shard must have its standbys. On the other hand, Distributed SQL has replication built into its distribution protocol to ensure high availability without additional complexity.

Regarding performance, I recommend against premature optimization, such as forcing tables and indexes together, as it can hinder elastic scaling and automatic rebalancing. The choice between Database Sharding and Distributed SQL depends on your needs. If you want each shard to be a genuine PostgreSQL database down to the storage, and your use-cases are single shards for writes workload and accept eventual consistency for cross-shard queries, go for Database Sharding. If you want a cloud-native OLTP database that scales without downtime, Distributed SQL makes it transparent to your application.

This reminds me of when database administrators used to split their databases manually across multiple physical disks. Still, Storage Area Networks (SAN) introduced the Stripe And Mirror Everything approach over the network. At first, people were worried about network latency, but ultimately, the benefits of high availability and operational flexibility won out. This agility is a must to keep cloud environments cost-effective.
